source.title: Embedding Comparator: Visualizing Differences in Global Structure and Local Neighborhoods via Small Multiples
source.authors: Angie Boggust; Brandon Carter; Arvind Satyanarayan

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present. The paper identifies itself as IUI ’22 (2022), while the supplied metadata says 2019.
record.tranche_reason: The study measures similarity between embedding spaces using Jaccard overlap of their k-nearest-neighbour sets. This bears on representation alignment, but it does not reproduce a scale-and-capability sweep.
record.gate_note: The paper reports local-neighbourhood similarities and qualitative comparisons across time periods, corpora, fine-tuning, and modalities. It does not compare alignment across model sizes or capability levels. Results cited from prior work are not recorded as findings here; user-study results about the visualization tool are also excluded.
record.test_reason: This is a visualization-tool paper (IUI '22). Its case studies compare embedding spaces with k-NN Jaccard overlap, but none bears on whether model representations converge. The HistWords decades differ by training text, so low overlap measures language change. The emoji 'image embedding' is raw pixels, not a learned vision model. Fine-tuning compares one model with itself. GloVe Wiki vs Twitter is a qualitative data-difference example with no similarity number. The k-variation shows which words rank highest, not whether measured convergence depends on k. The paper cites Convergent Learning (Li et al.) only in related work.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors conclude that their tool, built on reciprocal local-neighbourhood similarity, surfaces similarities and differences between embedding spaces without alignment, even across modalities. It also speeds up user insight compared with Jupyter, based on a first-use study with 15 participants. They make no claim about convergence.
record.recipe_differences: The study compares spaces using Jaccard overlap of k-nearest-neighbour sets, rather than testing representational alignment as a function of model scale or capability. Its focus is an interactive visualization system, not a reproduction of the cited convergence methods.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported examples depend on k: the paper highlights different high-similarity words at k=12 and k=100. It also reports different neighbourhood outcomes across compared corpora, time periods, and modalities. The emoji cluster pattern is said to persist across PCA, UMAP, and t-SNE.

fits_no_version.finding: k-NN Jaccard overlap between word embeddings trained on different decades of English is low. It is centred near 40% (1950s vs 1990s) and 18% (1800s vs 1990s), and falls as the time gap grows.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Neighbourhood overlap between same-method embeddings falls as their training corpora diverge.

fits_no_version.finding: Emoji2vec text embeddings and raw pixel vectors share few neighbours: most emojis are 0–10% similar, and none exceed 40%.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Learned semantic embeddings share little local structure with raw pixel space.

record.peer_reviewed: International Conference on Intelligent User Interfaces (IUI ’22)
record.problems: Claim-relevant comparisons are case studies, not controlled scale or capability sweeps. The study reports no uncertainty estimates for the similarity results and does not test alternative similarity functions, despite allowing users to select distance metrics. The emoji comparison has one paired dataset and does not establish whether alignment changes with model quality.
record.rows_left_out: No claim-relevant results were left out. Tool usability and participant study outcomes were excluded because they measure the visualization system rather than representation convergence.

untested.parts: No learned vision model and no quality comparison.
No mapping or stitching. Alignment is only discussed as something the tool avoids.
No test of how convergence estimates vary with metric, k or inputs.
No test of plateau or of shared data as the cause of alignment.

record.verdict_notes: The reader over-linked the rows to V6 and V7. The paper's comparisons are between differently trained data or time periods, against raw pixels, or before/after fine-tuning. None is a test of whether independently trained models converge. The study is reclassified as cites_only/T6, all rows are set to none, and the reader's labels are removed.

versions.untested_parts: No model-size or capability sweep; no test of whether alignment rises as models get larger or more capable.
The emoji case compares paired image and language embeddings, but does not compare models at different quality or test whether cross-modal alignment rises as both improve.
No comparison across random initializations of the same architecture.
The paper says its method does not require alignment, but does not test mapping, stitching, relative representations, or unpaired mapping.
No test of recurring interpretable features or circuits.
The paper varies neighbourhood size k and compares different datasets and modalities. It does not report a controlled comparison of alternative similarity functions, or an out-of-distribution test.

The study gives examples of incomplete similarity and training-data or modality differences, but does not test a plateau with scale or establish that shared data/objectives explain convergence rather than a common model of reality.

rows.subject: HistWords embeddings: 1900–1910 vs 1990–2000
rows.size_stated: 300-dimensional word2vec embeddings; 6121 shared words across the selected decades
rows.operation_detail: Compared per-word k-nearest-neighbour overlap and its distribution
rows.measure: Local neighbourhood similarity (Jaccard); distribution over words
rows.value: The similarity distribution is centered at 40%.
rows.note: The paper describes this as substantial dissimilarity across a 40-year interval; it does not report a scale or capability comparison.
rows.check: Compares embeddings trained on different decades' text. The 40% centre reflects language change, not model convergence. The text ties this figure to 1950s vs 1990s, not 1900s vs 1990s as the row says.

rows.subject: HistWords embeddings: 1800–1810 vs 1990–2000
rows.size_stated: 300-dimensional word2vec embeddings; 6121 shared words across the selected decades
rows.operation_detail: Compared per-word k-nearest-neighbour overlap and its distribution
rows.measure: Local neighbourhood similarity (Jaccard); distribution over words
rows.value: The distribution is centered at 18%, with very few words above 50% similarity.
rows.note: The result shows limited local-neighbourhood agreement for this pair, not a trend with model scale or performance.
rows.check: Diachronic data difference, not a test of representational convergence.

rows.subject: HistWords embeddings: decade comparisons against 1990–2000
rows.size_stated: 300-dimensional word2vec embeddings; 6121 shared words across the selected decades
rows.operation_detail: Compared similarity distributions across decade pairs
rows.value: The distribution shifts left as the compared decade gets earlier; the authors describe similarity as decreasing as the time between decades increases.
rows.note: The comparison concerns diachronic word embeddings, not model capability.
rows.check: Similarity falls with time gap between training corpora. This measures semantic drift, not convergence.

rows.subject: HistWords embeddings: 1900–1910 vs 1990–2000
rows.size_stated: 300-dimensional word2vec embeddings; 6121 shared words across the selected decades
rows.operation_detail: Changed k for the nearest-neighbour overlap comparison
rows.measure: Local neighbourhood similarity (Jaccard) for individual words
rows.value: “que” is described as having high similarity at this smaller k.
rows.note: The paper describes the French words as neighbours in both models despite the English training text.
rows.check: An example word highlighted at k=12. It does not show convergence estimates changing with k.

rows.subject: HistWords embeddings: 1900–1910 vs 1990–2000
rows.size_stated: 300-dimensional word2vec embeddings; 6121 shared words across the selected decades
rows.operation_detail: Changed k for the nearest-neighbour overlap comparison
rows.measure: Local neighbourhood similarity (Jaccard) for individual words
rows.value: Days and months, including “april” and “tuesday”, are described as having high similarity at this larger k.
rows.note: The paper interprets these as large neighbourhoods that remained consistent over time.
rows.check: An example word highlighted at k=100. Same issue as R4.

rows.subject: emoji2vec language embeddings vs raw emoji pixel embeddings
rows.size_stated: 300-dimensional language embeddings; 1296-dimensional pixel embeddings; 670 shared emojis
rows.stage_stated: pre-trained language embeddings; pixel values used as image embeddings
rows.operation_detail: Compared local-neighbourhood similarity for paired emoji images and textual descriptions

conditions.value: 670 emojis shared between emoji2vec and Apple emoji images

rows.measure: Local neighbourhood similarity (Jaccard); distribution over emojis
rows.value: Most emojis are 0–10% similar, and none are more than 40% similar.
rows.note: The authors interpret the low overlap as visual and semantic similarity often being disjoint. This is a single modality comparison, not a comparison of models as they improve.
rows.check: The image side is flattened raw RGBA pixels, not a trained vision model, so this cannot bear on V2 or V6.

rows.subject: emoji2vec language embeddings vs raw emoji pixel embeddings: baseball emoji
rows.stage_stated: pre-trained language embeddings; pixel values used as image embeddings
rows.operation_detail: Compared the nearest neighbours of the paired baseball emoji
rows.value: The language neighbours are sports-related; the pixel neighbours are similar in colour or shape. The only shared neighbour is a soccer ball.
rows.note: This is a per-object example of different neighbourhoods across the two modalities.

rows.subject: emoji2vec language embeddings vs raw emoji pixel embeddings: face emojis
rows.stage_stated: pre-trained language embeddings; pixel values used as image embeddings
rows.operation_detail: Compared locations and neighbourhoods of face and health-related emojis
rows.measure: Local neighbourhoods and projected cluster structure
rows.value: Face emojis form a tighter cluster in the image embedding space than health-related emojis do in the language embedding space; the cluster pattern is reported to persist across PCA, UMAP, and t-SNE.
rows.note: The paper attributes the contrast to faces being visually similar images and health-related emojis occurring in varied contexts.
rows.check: Projection-cluster observation against raw pixels. Not a convergence measure.

rows.subject: GloVe Wikipedia/newswire embeddings vs GloVe Twitter embeddings
rows.operation_detail: Compared local neighbourhoods of embeddings trained on different corpora
rows.measure: Local neighbourhood similarity and neighbour meanings
rows.value: The authors report that the models represent words differently; examples include slang, multilingual words, and popular-culture references differing across corpora.
rows.note: The paper explicitly relates the differences to the distinct training corpora.
rows.check: Qualitative only, with no similarity value. Reports corpus-specific word senses, not alignment between models.

rows.subject: GloVe Wikipedia/newswire embeddings vs GloVe Twitter embeddings
rows.operation_detail: Compared nearest neighbours for the word “def”
rows.value: In the Wikipedia/newswire model, “def” relates to defeat and sporting results; in the Twitter model, it relates to conversational terms such as “definitely” and “probably”.
rows.note: The pair comparison is presented as an effect of corpus differences.

rows.subject: GloVe Wikipedia/newswire embeddings vs GloVe Twitter embeddings
rows.value: “Solo” is related to Spanish words in Twitter but has its English meaning in Wikipedia/newswire; “swift” and “galaxy” refer to popular-culture entities in Twitter and different meanings in Wikipedia/newswire.
rows.locator: Appendix A.1; Figures A.1 and A.6
rows.note: Examples are reported separately in the paper as corpus-associated semantic differences.

rows.subject: fastText English embeddings before vs after sentiment fine-tuning
rows.stage_stated: pre-trained vs fine-tuned on movie-review sentiment data
rows.operation_detail: Compared neighbourhoods before and after task fine-tuning
rows.measure: Local neighbourhood similarity and neighbour meanings
rows.value: The paper reports a significant embedding-space change: sentiment-related words acquire sentiment-related neighbours, while some neutral words remain unchanged.
rows.note: This is evidence that fine-tuning can change the measured neighbourhoods; it does not test convergence with scale or capability.
rows.check: Before/after fine-tuning of the same embeddings. This concerns task-induced change, not convergence between independent models.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: HistWords comparisons with k=12 and k=100
reader_labels.reason: The reported high-similarity examples differ with neighbourhood size: “que” is highlighted at k=12, while days and months are highlighted at k=100 (R4–R5). The emoji and GloVe comparisons also show different similarity outcomes across inputs and training corpora (R6, R9–R11).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Compared diachronic, cross-modal, corpus-trained, and fine-tuned embeddings
reader_labels.reason: Similarity is incomplete in the reported comparisons, and the authors connect observed differences to elapsed time, modality, corpus, or fine-tuning rather than showing alignment as a general consequence of a shared model of reality (R1–R3, R6–R12).
